What decides the assessed value of a Missouri home?

Your county assessor lists every parcel each year and applies a fixed share of market value that varies by use. RSMo 137.115 sets houses and other residential land at 19%, farmland at 12% and commercial parcels at 32%. Tangible personal property is taxed on one third of its worth as of January 1.

Missouri revalues land and buildings every other year. The assessor determines fresh figures as of January 1 in odd-numbered years, and those figures stay on the books through the following even year, except that new construction and added improvements are picked up when completed. The latest reassessment year was 2025, which means a 2026 bill rests on that number. The next general revaluation is 2027. Counties can vote to opt out of the revaluation provisions, so the assessor's office is the place to confirm your county's schedule.

Residential owners get a safeguard against large jumps. If the assessor wants to raise a home's value more than fifteen percent over the previous one, aside from new construction, an on-site physical inspection must come first, and viewing from the street is not enough. You get at least thirty days to ask that the visit include the inside of the house. Anyone whose land is put to a different use may also ask the assessor to reclassify it.

When does a Missouri property tax bill have to be paid?

Payment goes to the county collector, and the last day is December 31. After that date the State Tax Commission says interest and penalties begin. Collectors can take cards and electronic payments, with any surcharge limited to what the card or payment company charges the county.

Planning a fall or winter sale? Call the collector for the parcel's current balance and ask whether older years are delinquent. Give that number to your closing agent before you agree to terms, so the amount does not catch you off guard at closing.

You need not wait to pay before challenging a value. The Commission's guidance allows an appeal even though the bill is still open. The cost of waiting is that unpaid tax keeps accumulating interest and penalties in the meantime.

How can an owner contest a Missouri property assessment?

The first stop is the board that equalizes values in your county, and the filing deadline there is the second Monday in July. A ruling against you can be taken to the State Tax Commission within thirty days of the date on the board's decision letter, using its Complaint for Review of Assessment.

Send the complaint through the Commission's online portal, by email to Legal@stc.mo.gov, or by mail to PO Box 146, Jefferson City, MO 65102-0146. Enclose the tax bill or the board's letter, and keep your other evidence for later in the process. Parcels titled to a corporation, LLC, limited partnership, trust or estate require an attorney to file, or the appeal will be rejected.

An owner may skip the county step and file straight with the Commission in two cases:

  • the assessor never gave the current owner notice of the value or of an increase at least thirty days ahead of the county deadline, including when the notice went to a prior owner;
  • the buyer closed within thirty days after the county mailed the tax statement.

Signing an agreed value with the assessor at the county stage ends the dispute for good. In a charter county or the City of St. Louis, a residential value produced by computer puts the burden on the assessor, who must present appraisal findings and three comparable sales.

What does it mean to pay Missouri property tax under protest?

It means you pay the whole bill on time while preserving your objection. Send the full amount to the collector before the December 31 cutoff, mark the check "paid under protest", and enclose a written statement of your grounds. When the complaint is about value, the statement has to state the market value you believe is right. A mailing postmarked on or before December 31 counts.

Doing neither carries a penalty. Per the Commission, an owner who paid without protest and filed no appeal by the deadline cannot contest that year's assessment. Next year is still open, because an appeal to the equalization board remains available on the same July date.

The takeaway for a seller is simple: the window is short, so mark the July date before you put the house on the market.

Appeal after a county ruling30 days from the letter dateState Tax Commission
Bill deadlineDecember 31State Tax Commission
Delinquent land saleFourth Monday in AugustRSMo 140.150

Is there tax relief for older or disabled Missouri homeowners?

The Department of Revenue administers a refundable credit known as the circuit breaker. It reimburses a slice of the real estate tax, or rent, that a qualifying senior or a person who is 100 percent disabled paid in the year. Homeowners who lived in their own home can receive up to $1,100, and renters up to $750. How much you actually get depends on what you paid and on all household income, taxable or not. Tenants of facilities that pay no property tax do not qualify.

Personal property tax questions belong with the county assessor. For the credit, the Department's page offers claim help and the address PropertyTaxCredit@dor.mo.gov. A homeowner thinking about selling can use those contacts to ask how moving would affect a claim.

What happens when Missouri property tax goes unpaid?

Delinquent parcels go to the collector's sale on the fourth Monday in August. RSMo 140.150 directs the collector to mail the record owner a first notice, then a certified second notice if the assessed value tops $1,000. An owner who never receives the mail still owes the tax, and payment to the collector is accepted until the moment of sale.

Once a sale happens, RSMo 140.340 lets the owner, a lienholder, an occupant or any other interested party redeem without question during the following year. After that, redemption stays possible, though defeasible, until the purchaser obtains the deed. The price includes the purchase money and sale costs, certificate interest capped at ten percent a year, and any later taxes the purchaser advanced plus eight percent interest on them.

If you owe back taxes and want to sell, ask the collector for a full payoff with interest before August. A sold certificate adds costs to everything that follows.

More questions about Missouri Property Tax Guide

What share of a home's value is taxed in Missouri?

Nineteen percent. RSMo 137.115 assesses residential real property at 19% of true value, farmland at 12% and commercial property at 32%.

By what date must a value appeal be filed locally?

The second Monday in July is the filing date at the county equalization board. If the board denies the appeal, the State Tax Commission accepts a complaint within thirty days of the date on the decision letter.

Must the bill be paid first if I plan to appeal?

No. The State Tax Commission says an appeal is allowed while taxes are unpaid. Interest and penalties still build after December 31, so many owners instead pay under protest and file the written statement with the collector.

Is my home revalued each year in Missouri?

Not every year. New values are set in odd-numbered years and stay for the next even year, apart from new construction and improvements. 2025 was the latest general reassessment and 2027 is the next.

Who can claim the Missouri circuit breaker credit?

Certain seniors and people who are 100 percent disabled. The top credit is $1,100 for owner-occupants and $750 for renters, and the exact figure turns on tax or rent paid and total household income.

Does Missouri have a homestead exemption?

Missouri homeowners meet three separate things that people often lump together under the homestead name: a state income-based property tax credit, a county option credit for owners 62 and older, and a creditor protection under RSMo 513.475 that shields part of a home's value from judgment collection.

Which of the three matters depends on whether the question is a tax bill, a lender or judgment creditor, or a sale. Each has its own agency, its own form and its own eligibility test, so it helps to sort them before filing anything.

What is the Missouri Property Tax Credit Claim?

It is the state's "circuit breaker," run by the Department of Revenue. The credit goes to certain senior citizens and to individuals who are 100 percent disabled, covering part of the real estate tax or rent paid for the year. The maximum is $750 for renters and $1,100 for owners who owned and occupied their home.

The department's frequently asked questions set household income caps that vary with ownership and filing status. Owners who occupied the home all year must be at $30,000 or less if single, or $34,000 or less if married filing combined. Renters and part-year owners face lower caps of $27,200 single and $29,200 married filing combined. Household income is broad: it adds Social Security, pensions, public assistance, child support and similar receipts to Missouri adjusted income.

How do I claim the credit?

The route depends on whether a Missouri income tax return is required. Filers use Form MO-1040 with the Property Tax Schedule (MO-PTS) attached, and anyone not required to file uses the stand-alone Form MO-PTC. The department says a claim for a past year can still be filed for three years after its original due date, while the 2025 claim was due April 15, 2026.

  • Bring the paid real estate tax receipt from the county collector.
  • Add every W-2 and 1099, and benefit letters where they apply.
  • Include Form 948 from the assessor if the property has more than five acres, since the credit counts the tax on five acres and the home.
  • Claim a tax bill in the year you paid it. A 2025 bill paid in 2026 goes on the 2025 claim.

The credit applies only to a home the claimant occupies, and only where property tax is actually paid on it. Sewer lateral charges, penalties and interest do not count.

What is the Missouri homestead tax credit for owners 62 and older?

It is a county option. RSMo 137.1050 lets a county that can levy a property tax grant a credit to residents who are at least 62, are owners of record or hold a legal or equitable interest shown in a written instrument, and are liable for the tax on a home they occupy as their primary residence. A county turns the credit on by ordinance or by a vote after a petition signed by at least five percent of the registered voters who voted in the last governor's race.

The credit equals the amount by which the owner's real property tax has risen since the owner's initial credit year. If new construction is added to the home, or the home is annexed into a new taxing district, the starting amount is raised to match. The county collector shows the credit on the tax statement, and the county tells each political subdivision the total by November 30 each year. To find out whether your county has adopted it, ask the county collector or assessor.

How does Missouri assess a home for tax purposes?

Residential real property is assessed at nineteen percent of true value in money, according to RSMo 137.115. Agricultural land is assessed at twelve percent, and commercial property at thirty-two percent. New values are set as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year and carry into the even-numbered year that follows, except for new construction.

The same statute requires a physical inspection before an assessor raises a residential parcel's value by more than fifteen percent from the last assessment, not counting new construction. The owner gets written notice and can ask, within thirty days, for an interior inspection. A drive-by does not count. An owner whose use of the property changes can ask the assessor to reclassify it.

What does the homestead creditor protection do?

RSMo 513.475 exempts a person's dwelling and the land used with it from attachment and execution, up to an aggregate value. The version of the section that takes effect on January 1, 2027 sets that value at $40,000, after a 2026 amendment. Where several owners of one homestead claim the exemption, together they cannot exceed the single total.

The section also bars either spouse from selling, mortgaging or otherwise transferring the homestead alone. A sale or mortgage is valid when husband and wife convey jointly. The statute calls a sale by one spouse alone null and void, so both spouses sign the deed when the house is their homestead.

Where do I get help with the credit paperwork?

The Department of Revenue runs a claim assistance page and answers questions at PropertyTaxCredit@dor.mo.gov. Proof of Social Security or Supplemental Security Income benefits can come from a my Social Security account online or by calling the Social Security Administration, while the SSA-1099 form still arrives by mail. The county collector holds the paid-tax receipt, and the assessor supplies Form 948 for parcels of more than five acres.

How do the Missouri home tax breaks compare?

ProgramWho qualifiesWhat it does

County homestead credit (137.1050)Owner-occupants 62 or older in a county that adopted itCredit for the increase in tax since the initial credit year
Creditor homestead (513.475)Any owner who uses the home as a homesteadExempts up to $40,000 in value from execution, effective January 1, 2027
Residential assessment (137.115)All owners of residential real propertyAssessed at 19 percent of true value

How does selling a home affect these tax breaks?

A sale in the middle of a year can lower what you may claim. Anyone who owned the home for only part of the year uses the lower part-year income caps, and the credit is limited to a home the claimant occupies. Keep the settlement statement and the paid tax receipt for the year of sale, since the claim asks for the real estate tax you paid.

Ask the county collector how the tax for the year of sale will be split on the closing statement, and whether the county has adopted the credit for owners 62 and older.

More questions about Missouri Homestead Exemption

What is the Missouri property tax credit worth?

Up to $1,100 for an owner who owned and occupied the home, and up to $750 for a renter, according to the <a href="https://dor.mo.gov/taxation/individual/tax-types/property-tax-credit/">Department of Revenue</a>. The actual figure depends on tax or rent paid and total household income.

What is the income limit for the Missouri property tax credit?

For owners who lived in their home all year, $30,000 if single and $34,000 if married filing combined. Renters and part-year owners are limited to $27,200 single and $29,200 married filing combined, per the department's <a href="https://dor.mo.gov/faq/taxation/individual/property-tax-credit-claim.html">FAQ page</a>.

At what age can I get the county homestead credit?

Sixty-two. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=137.1050">RSMo 137.1050</a> sets that minimum, and it applies only in a county that has adopted the credit by ordinance or vote. Ask your county collector whether yours has.

Does the homestead protection stop me from selling my house?

No. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=513.475">RSMo 513.475</a> protects the home from execution up to a value cap and says spouses must convey jointly. A joint deed by husband and wife is allowed.

Can I still file for the credit after I sell the house?

The department allows a claim for a past year up to three years after its original due date. A claim covers real estate tax paid on a home you occupied, and a part-year owner uses the lower income caps.

Does Missouri charge an estate tax?

Missouri imposes no estate tax for any death since the start of 2005, and no state return has to be filed for those deaths. The revenue department explains that the state tax was tied to a federal credit, and the IRS stopped allowing that credit for deaths after 2004.

The mechanism is in RSMo 145.011. It taxes the transfer of an estate with Missouri tax situs at the maximum state death tax credit under Internal Revenue Code Section 2011. Federal law stepped that credit down to 75 percent for 2002 deaths, 50 percent for 2003, 25 percent for 2004 and nothing afterward, which leaves the Missouri figure at zero. If the IRS ever brings the credit back, a Missouri return would be due again under sections 145.011 to 145.955.

Is there a federal estate tax that could reach a Missouri house?

Federal estate tax reaches only estates above the basic exclusion amount, which the IRS sets at $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths under the law signed on July 4, 2025. Most family homes in Missouri fall far below that line. A married couple can also carry over an unused exclusion to the surviving spouse by electing portability on a timely filed return.

  • 2022 deaths: $12,060,000
  • 2023 deaths: $12,920,000
  • 2024 deaths: $13,610,000
  • 2025 deaths: $13,990,000
  • 2026 deaths: $15,000,000

These are the IRS's published basic exclusion amounts by year of death. An estate over the threshold files Form 706. When the executor files one, beneficiaries generally get a Schedule A on Form 8971 reporting the estate tax value of what they received, and certain beneficiaries must use that figure as initial basis.

How can heirs get an inherited Missouri house sold?

Which path fits depends on how big the estate is and whether a personal representative has been appointed. Two paths in the Missouri statutes cover most house sales by heirs.

Two Missouri routes to selling a decedent's real estate, based on the revisor's statutes
RouteWhat triggers itStatute
Small estate affidavitNet estate of $40,000 or less after liens and debts, thirty days since the death, and no pending or granted application for lettersRSMo 473.097
Petition to sellAn executor or administrator asks the probate court for authority to sell real property of the estateRSMo 473.493

On the small estate route, distributees show title by recording a copy of the affidavit and the clerk's certificate in every county that holds part of the land. The person signing the affidavit posts a bond unless the court waives it and pays the filing fee. If the listed property tops $15,000, the clerk runs a creditor notice two weeks in a row.

What does a court-ordered sale look like?

When letters have issued, RSMo 473.493 lets the executor or administrator file a petition stating why the sale is needed and describing the property. The court schedules a hearing and sends notice, by regular mail or publication, to heirs and devisees named in the file and to others the court names.

  • If the court orders publication, the notice runs weekly for four straight weeks.
  • The hearing then falls no earlier than the thirtieth day and no later than the forty-second day after the first insertion.
  • With satisfactory proof at the hearing, the court may approve a sale of the whole property or a piece of it.
  • When a mortgage secures a claim that is due, the court may order a sale subject to the mortgage with the lender's consent, and that consent releases the estate from any later deficiency.

Your probate attorney will tell you whether a petition is needed or whether the will already gives the personal representative power to sell.

Do heirs need an IRS closing letter or basis statement before a sale?

Only estates that must file Form 706 deal with these items. For those estates, Section 6035 requires the executor to send statements to the IRS and to beneficiaries who receive certain property, and Section 1014(f) requires the beneficiary's basis to stay consistent with the value finally determined for federal estate tax. The IRS issued final regulations on this consistent basis reporting on September 16, 2024.

An estate that is not required to file a return should not send Form 8971, because the IRS warns that doing so may cause unnecessary correspondence.

An executor who wants proof that the federal case is closed can request the Estate Tax Closing Letter, Letter 627. The IRS raised the user fee for that letter from $56 to $76 on October 26, 2026, so the higher amount now applies. Heirs waiting on a sale of the family house should ask the executor whether a return was filed and, if so, request their Schedule A before closing so the basis figure is on paper.

What tax do heirs pay after selling an inherited Missouri house?

The federal gain is the sale price less basis, and basis for inherited property is generally the house's worth when the owner died, under IRS Publication 551. A house worth $200,000 at death and sold for $205,000 shows $5,000 of gain, regardless of what the original owner paid decades earlier. The IRS directs readers who inherited property to Publication 551 and to Topic 409 for holding period details.

On the state side, Missouri lets an individual subtract all federally reported capital gains when computing the state return. That subtraction is available to individuals and not to trusts, so who holds title when the sale closes matters. If the sale happens inside the estate, ask the preparer how the estate's income is reported.

Missouri imposes a fiduciary income tax on income earned by an estate or trust. A resident estate that must file federal Form 1041 files a Missouri fiduciary return, and a nonresident estate must file when it has $600 or more of Missouri-source gross income.

What paperwork should heirs gather before listing?

  • A certified death certificate, since the date of death anchors the basis figure.
  • Letters testamentary or of administration, or the small estate affidavit with the clerk's certificate.
  • An appraisal or other documented fair market value as of the date of death.
  • The current deed, which carries the legal description the recorder will need.
  • Any Schedule A from Form 8971, if the estate filed a federal return.
  • Payoff figures for any mortgage, unpaid tax or lien.

A deed goes on file with the recorder of the county that holds the land under RSMo 442.380. RSMo 442.400 adds that an unrecorded instrument is valid only between the parties and anyone with actual notice, so the buyer's deed should be filed promptly. A probate attorney near the decedent's home court can confirm the filing order for your estate.

More questions about Missouri Estate and Inheritance Tax

Is there a Missouri estate tax for deaths in 2026?

No. The revenue department reports that no Missouri estate tax applies to any death since 2005, and no return is required. A return would be required again only if the IRS reinstated the federal state death tax credit.

How large must an estate be before federal estate tax applies?

For 2026 deaths the IRS basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000. An estate below that amount owes no federal estate tax, although a surviving spouse may still file to elect portability of an unused amount.

Can heirs sell a Missouri house without opening probate?

Sometimes. When the net estate is $40,000 or under, thirty days have gone by and no one has sought letters, distributees can use the small estate affidavit in RSMo 473.097 and file it with the recorder.

What is the tax basis of a house I inherited?

Generally what it was worth at the owner's death, or on the alternate valuation date if the estate chose one. Beneficiaries of an estate that filed Form 706 usually receive a Schedule A with the value.

Does Missouri tax the gain when an heir sells an inherited house?

Eligible individuals may subtract all federally reported capital gains on the state return, using Form MO-A with Form MO-1040. Trusts cannot claim that subtraction.

What are the steps of a Missouri eviction case?

A Missouri rent and possession case moves through five stages: a verified filing, a summons, a hearing, a judgment with a ten day window, and an officer's writ. Chapter 535 of the Missouri statutes lays out each stage, and the whole path runs through the associate circuit court of the county where the rented house sits.

A landlord who is not claiming unpaid rent follows a different path under chapter 534, the unlawful detainer statutes, which covers tenants who hold over after a lease ends, occupants after a foreclosure, and employees who stay after a job that came with housing ends (RSMo 534.030). The sections below follow the rent case, since that is the filing a rental owner sees most.

How does a landlord start the case?

By filing a statement under oath. RSMo 535.020 calls for an affidavit filed with an associate circuit judge that gives the rental terms, the rent actually due, the fact that payment was demanded and not made, and a description of the property. Local court rules may route these filings to one central location in the county, so the clerk can say where the paperwork goes.

Once the statement is in, the clerk issues a summons naming the tenant and every person occupying the home, ordering them to appear and show cause why possession should not go back to the landlord. The case is then handled under the Missouri rules of civil procedure except where chapter 535 says otherwise.

How is the tenant served and how soon is the hearing?

Service has to happen at least four days before the court date, and the court date in the summons cannot be more than twenty-one business days after the summons issues unless the landlord agrees in writing to a later date. That is the rule in RSMo 535.030.

If the tenant cannot be found, the landlord may ask for service by posting a copy of the summons and complaint on the dwelling and mailing a copy by ordinary mail, both at least ten days before the court date. A tenant served this way who does not show up can still lose possession, but the statute bars a money judgment against that tenant unless the tenant has entered an appearance.

When the tenant does appear, RSMo 535.040 has the judge set the case on the first available date. If the rent was demanded, is still unpaid, and the tenant does not tender the rent and costs in court, the judge enters judgment for possession plus the rent due and court costs.

What happens in the days after a judgment?

The tenant has ten days from judgment to ask the court to set it aside or to apply for a trial de novo, according to RSMo 535.030. Without one of those filings the judgment for possession becomes final and the tenant can be removed with no further notice. When the tenant was in default, the clerk mails a notice of that ten day window to the last known address.

  • Execution. The judge issues an execution that commands an officer to put the landlord in possession, and the officer must deliver possession within five days of receiving it (RSMo 535.040).
  • Seven day fallback. If the officer has not delivered possession seven days after the writ reached the officer, the landlord has sixty days from the judgment to act with a municipal or county officer present, without breaching the peace (RSMo 441.060).
  • Paperwork. The landlord must show the officer a true copy of the judgment and execution, get the officer's written acknowledgment, and file that acknowledgment in court within five days after taking possession.

Which Missouri cases are not rent cases?

Chapter 534 covers a holdover after a lease ends, an occupant who stays after a foreclosure, an employee who stays after housing tied to the job ends, and a person who took possession wrongfully and refuses a written demand to leave (RSMo 534.030). The remedy is an unlawful detainer action.

Occupancy is a separate topic. RSMo 441.060 presumes that a limit of two persons per bedroom is reasonable, and the limit does not apply to a child born to the tenants during the lease.

What happens to the tenant's belongings and the deposit?

Under RSMo 535.040 a landlord is not liable for goods left in the home after a court-ordered execution unless the landlord acted willfully, wantonly or maliciously. One exception applies: when an item carries a conspicuous permanent label showing it belongs to a third party, the landlord must send certified mail, return receipt requested, and give that party five business days after receipt to pick it up.

Deposits follow RSMo 535.300. A landlord may not take more than two months' rent as a deposit, has to hold it in an insured bank or credit union, and has thirty days after the tenancy ends to return it or mail an itemized list of damages along with the balance. A landlord who wrongfully withholds any part owes the tenant twice the amount withheld.

What should an owner who wants to sell a rented house do during an eviction?

Keep the case file in order and tell any buyer where the case stands. A buyer who is paying cash for a house with a pending eviction needs the filing date, the court date, and a copy of any judgment.

  • Do not change locks, remove doors or shut off utilities. Section 441.233 treats that as forcible entry and detainer.
  • Keep the demand, the affidavit, proof of service and the judgment together in one folder.
  • Ask the circuit clerk for the case number and the next court date, and share them with the title company.
  • Close on a date that follows the ten day window, since a judgment is not final before then.

If the sale closes before the case ends, the contract should say plainly who handles the case and the tenant afterward.

More questions about Missouri Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Missouri eviction take?

The statutes set a hearing within twenty-one business days of the summons unless the landlord agrees to later, plus a ten day window after judgment and up to five days for the officer to deliver possession. Those limits come from <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.030">RSMo 535.030</a> and <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.040">RSMo 535.040</a>. Local court calendars and appeals add to the total.

Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying the rent in court?

Yes, if the rent and costs are tendered before the judge at the hearing. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.040">RSMo 535.040</a> directs the judge to enter a possession judgment only when that payment has not been made.

What if the tenant never shows up in court?

The judge can still hear the case. When the tenant was served by posting and mailing, the landlord can win possession but the court may not grant a money judgment against a tenant in default, as <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.030">RSMo 535.030</a> provides.

Can the landlord keep the tenant's security deposit to cover unpaid rent?

Yes, to the extent reasonably necessary. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=535.300">RSMo 535.300</a> lets the landlord withhold for unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear, and losses from short notice, and requires an itemized list within thirty days of the end of the tenancy.

Can a landlord do a lockout instead of going to court?

No. <a href="https://revisor.mo.gov/main/OneSection.aspx?section=441.233">RSMo 441.233</a> treats removing a tenant or the tenant's property without a court order, taking off doors or locks, or willfully cutting essential services as forcible entry and detainer.

What rules apply to a quitclaim deed in Missouri?

A quitclaim deed is a conveyance of land, so it falls under the same execution and recording rules that Chapter 442 sets for every deed in the state. The Missouri statutes name quitclaim deeds directly in a few places, including the offense of filing false documents, which lists a warranty, special or quitclaim deed among the instruments it covers.

Two things control whether the paper works. First, it has to be signed and acknowledged the way the statute demands. Second, it has to be recorded with the recorder of deeds covering the land, in a format the recorder will accept.

Before you sign one, decide whether the transfer is final and whether you are giving up a say in a later sale. Your title company can tell you what it will want to see.

Who has to sign, and what must the deed say?

RSMo 442.130 requires every deed or conveyance of land to be subscribed by the person granting it, or by a lawful agent, and acknowledged or proved and certified. The statute also says that any written instrument conveying real estate must state whether each natural person acting as a grantor, mortgagor or other executing party is married or unmarried. An omission of marital status is a common reason a recorder pushes a deed back.

The recording statute adds a first-page checklist. Beneath a three-inch blank margin at the top, RSMo 59.310 expects the following:

  • the title of the document and its date;
  • every grantor's name and marital status;
  • every grantee's name;
  • any statutory addresses;
  • the legal description of the property;
  • book and page references where a statute calls for them.

If the first page does not have room, the page where the missing information appears must be stated there. Use the legal description from your existing deed, not just the street address, since the address alone is not a legal description.

Where do you record a Missouri quitclaim deed?

The deed goes to the recorder of deeds for the county that holds the parcel. RSMo 442.380 says an instrument that conveys real estate, once proved or acknowledged and certified in the prescribed manner, goes into the books of the recorder in the county in which the real estate lies.

The state also sets what a recorder may collect. Recording a deed or other instrument costs five dollars for page one and three dollars per page beyond it. A certified or sealed copy and a plain copy have their own separate fees listed in the same statute. The recorder may charge an extra $25 when a document does not meet the format standards but is accepted anyway.

Some documents are exempt from the format rules, among them papers signed before January 1, 2002, certified copies and documents executed outside the United States. If a recorder rejects your deed, the statute requires it to be returned to the preparer or presenter with an explanation of why it could not be recorded. Ask your recorder whether it accepts documents submitted electronically, because the statutes leave that choice to each office.

What format does the recorder require?

The format rules are detailed, and a recorder is allowed to turn a deed away for missing them. Under RSMo 59.310 the recorder may refuse a document that does not follow them:

  • one or more individual pages printed on one side only, not permanently bound and not in continuous form;
  • type no smaller than eight point, in black or dark ink;
  • white or light-colored paper of at least twenty-pound weight, free of watermarks;
  • signatures in black or dark ink, with the signer's name typed, printed or stamped beneath;
  • a top margin of at least three inches reserved for the recorder, and margins of at least three-fourths of an inch on every other side.

Nonessential items such as form numbers or customer notations may go in the margin. A document that is hard to read must be accompanied by an exact typed copy in eight-point type or larger. Staples that hold pages together are allowed, but attachments should be avoided unless a statute requires them.

Which Missouri deed rules are easy to overlook?

What happens when a deed names more than one grantee?

The wording of the grantee clause decides how the new owners hold title. RSMo 442.450 says an interest granted to two or more persons is a tenancy in common unless the grant expressly declares joint tenancy. The exceptions are executors and trustees and husband and wife, which the statute treats separately. A court annotation to that section shows how it can go wrong: a deed written by a layperson that used the phrase "tenants by entirety and to the survivor of them" for a mother and daughter was held to create a joint tenancy.

The practical lesson is to say what you mean in plain terms and to avoid mixing labels. When siblings take an inherited house, tenancy in common is the default, and each co-owner can usually be asked to sign before a sale. If the intent is survivorship, the deed has to say so.

If the owner has died, a quitclaim from the heirs is not the only route. A deed that states it takes effect on the owner's death can be recorded during life under RSMo 461.025, and a small estate affidavit can be recorded afterward. Which one fits depends on facts a title company will want to see.

What are the risks of using a quitclaim deed in a sale?

The risk is less about the form itself and more about what is attached to the property and who signed. Missouri treats a false or forged deed seriously. Under RSMo 570.095, a person who files or presents a deed with the intent to defraud, knowing it contains materially false information, is a forgery or lacks the consent of every party, commits the offense of filing false documents. A first offense is a class D felony, and the court must order restitution.

The same statute gives property owners a remedy. Anyone who believes a recorded document is fraudulent can file a probable cause statement with the associate or circuit court serving the recording county. The first hearing must be set within twenty business days, and a ruling of invalid can be recorded at no filing fee.

For sellers, the sensible approach is to treat a quitclaim as one step in a title chain. Have the title company look over the vesting deed, any lien and the proposed grantee before you sign, and send the finished deed to the recorder instead of holding it in a drawer.

More questions about Missouri Quitclaim Deed

Does a Missouri quitclaim deed need to be notarized?

It must be acknowledged or proved and certified. RSMo 442.130 requires the grantor, or a lawful agent, to sign, and the signature must be acknowledged or proved and certified in the manner the statute prescribes. Ask the recorder or your title company which officer can take the acknowledgment.

What will the recorder charge to file a Missouri deed?

The statutory charge is $5 for page one and $3 for every added page. A document that breaks the format rules but is accepted anyway carries a $25 surcharge under RSMo 59.310. Ask the recorder about copy fees.

Do I have to state if the grantor is married?

Yes. Every written instrument conveying real estate must state whether each natural person signing as a grantor is married or unmarried, and the first page of a recorded document must show each grantor's name and marital status.

Which office files a Missouri deed?

The county recorder of deeds for the place the land is located. RSMo 442.380 sends instruments that convey real estate to that county's recorder.

What if two people receive property by one quitclaim deed?

They hold as tenants in common unless the deed expressly declares a joint tenancy. RSMo 442.450 makes that the rule for two or more grantees other than executors, trustees and husband and wife.

How does a Missouri beneficiary deed work?

Missouri's version is called a beneficiary deed, and it hands real estate to a named person at the owner's death without a probate case for that property. Section 461.025 of the Nonprobate Transfers Law describes it as a deed to a designated grantee that says outright that it does not take effect until the owner dies.

Two conditions make it work. The deed has to be signed and filed of record, before the owner's death, in each county or city where the land lies. And it must contain the express statement that it takes effect only on death. The statute adds that the deed needs no consideration and need not be delivered to the beneficiary, and that the beneficiary can be a trust whether or not the trust is revocable.

A deed that is not recorded until after the owner's death is not automatically void. Section 461.025 says it does not invalidate any deed that is otherwise effective by law to pass title, even if recorded late. The beneficiary deed itself, though, only qualifies under this section when it is filed before death.

Can the owner still sell or change the property while alive?

Yes. The beneficiary gets no rights in the property during the owner's lifetime, and the beneficiary's signature is never needed for anything the owner wants to do with the house. That rule is in section 461.031.

The rules for changing or cancelling the designation sit in section 461.033:

  • An owner may revoke or change a beneficiary designation in whole or in part at any time before death.
  • When joint owners are involved, a change needs the agreement of every owner still living.
  • A later designation replaces an earlier one unless it says otherwise.
  • A will cannot undo a beneficiary designation unless the designation itself gave the owner the right to revoke by will.
  • Selling or giving away the property during life ends the designation for that property.

That last point matters to a homeowner thinking of selling. A recorded beneficiary deed does not stop you from listing the house, taking a cash offer and closing, and the sale ends the beneficiary's claim to the parcel sold.

What happens to the property when the owner dies?

The house passes by operation of law to the beneficiary, with no court order needed for the transfer itself (section 461.031). If two or more beneficiaries survive, they hold separate shares as tenants in common, and no survivorship right runs between them unless the deed expressly provides one. A share belonging to a beneficiary who later dies goes to that person's estate.

When no beneficiary survives the owner, the property belongs to the owner's estate instead. Where joint owners made the designation together, the surviving joint owner takes the property when the first one dies.

Does divorce or a creditor claim affect a Missouri beneficiary deed?

Both can. Under section 461.051, if the owner's marriage ends in divorce or annulment after the designation, any provision in favor of the former spouse, or of a relative of the former spouse, is revoked on the date the marriage ends. The designation is read as though that person had disclaimed. The revocation does not apply if the designation was made irrevocable, was made after the divorce, or says expressly that a divorce does not affect it. Remarrying the former spouse revives the provision.

Creditors keep some reach. Section 461.071 gives a deceased owner's creditors, surviving spouse and unmarried minor children the rights set out in section 461.300 against the value of property that passed outside probate. That means a beneficiary who receives a house may be asked to contribute toward statutory allowances and claims if the probate estate cannot cover them.

Anyone who inherits a house this way and plans to sell it quickly should ask the probate division clerk in the county whether any estate has been opened, since an open estate or a creditor claim could slow the closing.

When can a small estate affidavit replace a deed?

If no beneficiary deed exists and the whole estate is small, heirs may claim the real estate with an affidavit instead of a full administration. Section 473.097 sets the test:

  • The estate, after subtracting liens, debts and encumbrances, is worth no more than $40,000.
  • A month has gone by since the death, and nobody has applied for letters or been granted them.
  • The person making the affidavit files a bond approved by the probate judge or clerk, unless the court decides a bond is unnecessary.
  • The filing fee set by section 483.580 is paid, along with any required creditor notice publication cost.

The affidavit itemizes the property with values, names the people who will receive each item, and swears that debts will be paid. The clerk attaches a certificate. Heirs then prove their right to real estate by recording both papers in every county that holds a piece of it. If the itemized property tops $15,000, the clerk runs a creditor notice in a local paper for two straight weeks.

Property that the decedent held as a tenant by the entirety or joint tenant is left out of the affidavit's list. An estate above the $40,000 limit does not qualify, which is one reason owners record a beneficiary deed while they are alive.

What changes when the new owner wants to sell?

Once title has passed, the beneficiary owns the property outright and can sell it like any other owner. A buyer's closing agent will want the recorded beneficiary deed and proof that the former owner has died. Ask the county recorder what they require to place a death certificate or similar proof on record in your county, because the statute does not list that step.

Where the owner left no deed, the heirs usually need a probate case or a small estate affidavit first. Our Missouri recording guide explains page format, fees and acknowledgment for the deeds that will follow, and the Missouri probate laws page covers what happens when an estate has to be opened.

Check the property tax bill early. Learn the parcel's current tax balance from the county collector before any offer is signed.

More questions about Missouri Transfer on Death Deed

Does a Missouri beneficiary deed skip probate?

For the property it names, yes. Under section 461.025 the house passes to the designated beneficiary at the owner's death when the deed was on file beforehand. Other assets may still need probate.

Must the beneficiary sign or accept a Missouri beneficiary deed?

No. Section 461.025 says the deed needs no consideration and need not be delivered to the beneficiary, and section 461.031 says the beneficiary's signature is never required for the owner's transactions.

Can I cancel a Missouri beneficiary deed?

Yes, at any time before death. Section 461.033 lets the owner revoke or change it, though joint owners must all agree, and a will cannot revoke it unless the deed allows that. A later designation replaces the earlier one.

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner in Missouri?

The designation fails for that person. If no beneficiary survives the owner, section 461.031 says the property belongs to the owner's estate, which then goes through the usual estate process.

How big can a Missouri estate be for the small estate affidavit?

The value of the entire estate, less liens, debts and encumbrances, may not exceed $40,000. Section 473.097 also requires thirty days since the death and no pending application for letters.

Does Missouri tax the profit from selling a home?

For individuals, Missouri now lets you subtract 100 percent of federally reported capital gains from federal adjusted gross income on the state return, so the profit on a house sale is effectively not taxed by Missouri. The authority is Section 143.121 RSMo, added by House Bill 594.

The revenue department announced the change on August 26, 2025, describing Missouri as the first state to fully exempt capital gains tax for individual filers. The release says individuals can deduct all capital gains reported for federal purposes, short term and long term, from assets such as stocks, real estate and cryptocurrency, starting with the 2025 tax year. Federal tax is a separate matter and still applies to the gain.

How do you claim the Missouri capital gains subtraction?

You claim it on Form MO-A, filed with your Form MO-1040 individual income tax return. The amount comes from the capital gain portion of your federal return. For the 2025 tax year the department says the figure is the amount on line 7a of federal Form 1040.

One wrinkle needs attention. The department's FAQ opens by calling the subtraction effective for the 2025 tax year, yet a later answer says it applies to years starting in 2026 and can first be claimed on the 2026 return filed in 2027. If you sold a house in 2025, confirm with the department which return carries the subtraction before you file.

Married couples need care when only one spouse has a gain. The department's example shows a combined $10,000 on line 7a made of a $5,000 loss for one spouse and a $15,000 gain for the other. The $10,000 goes on the MO-A line for the spouse who had the gain, and nothing goes on the other spouse's line.

Who cannot use the Missouri subtraction?

The subtraction is written for individuals subject to tax under section 143.011. The department's answers draw several lines:

  • Trusts cannot claim it, because a fiduciary is not an individual subject to that section.
  • A pass-through entity that pays pass-through entity tax cannot claim it.
  • Corporations are excluded for now. They may subtract 100 percent of capital gains in the tax year after Missouri's top individual rate falls to 4.5 percent or lower, and the top rate for 2025 is 4.7 percent.
  • Capital losses do not qualify. The subtraction reaches only federally reported capital gains, and allowed losses already reduce federal adjusted gross income.

If your house is held in a trust or an LLC taxed as a pass-through, talk to a tax preparer before you list it.

What federal tax is due on a Missouri house sale?

On the sale of your main home, the IRS lets you leave out $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return. Two tests apply. You need 24 months of ownership and 24 months of living there as a residence, both inside the 5 years ending on the sale date, and the two stretches need not line up. A person who already excluded gain on a different home within the previous two years generally cannot use it again.

A Form 1099-S in your mailbox means the sale goes on the return even if the whole gain is excludable. Any taxable portion is reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D. The IRS says the tax rate on most net long-term gain is no higher than 15 percent for most individuals in 2025, with 0 percent at lower incomes and 20 percent for the highest incomes. Property kept a year or less produces short-term gain, taxed like wages. Depreciation recapture on a rental, called unrecaptured section 1250 gain, tops out at 25 percent.

How do the Missouri and federal pieces fit together?

Missouri and federal tax pieces for a home sale, with the agency that publishes each rule
QuestionAnswerWhere it comes from
Missouri tax on capital gain for individualsSubtract 100% of federally reported gainMissouri Department of Revenue, section 143.121
Form for the Missouri subtractionMO-A with MO-1040Missouri Department of Revenue FAQ
Missouri top individual rate, 20254.7%Missouri Department of Revenue
Federal home sale exclusion$250,000, or $500,000 on a joint returnIRS Topic 701
Federal ownership and use tests24 months each within the last 5 yearsIRS Topic 701
Federal long-term rates in 20250%, 15% and 20% by incomeIRS Topic 409
Forms to report the saleForm 8949 and Schedule DIRS Topic 409

Because Missouri follows your federal figures, an accurate federal return is the starting point for everything on the state side.

Do estimated payments or surtaxes follow a large home sale?

A taxable gain on a house can trigger a quarterly estimated tax obligation on the federal side, since the IRS says a taxpayer with a taxable capital gain may be required to make estimated payments. Its Publication 505 explains how to decide whether you must. Individuals with significant investment income can also owe the net investment income tax, which the IRS describes in Topic 559.

Losses work differently. The IRS does not allow a deduction for a loss on a home you lived in. For other capital assets, a net capital loss can reduce income by up to $3,000 a year ($1,500 if married filing separately), with the rest carried forward. A seller who lived in the house and is selling at a loss has nothing to claim for the house itself, and the Missouri subtraction cannot turn a loss into a deduction either.

Sellers who rented out the house for part of their ownership should ask a preparer how the rental years affect the exclusion and any depreciation recapture before listing.

How is the gain figured when you inherited the house?

Your gain equals the amount realized minus adjusted basis. For an inherited house, IRS Publication 551 says basis is generally what the house was worth when the owner died, or its worth on the alternate valuation date if the estate chose one. If a federal estate tax return was required, the executor hands each beneficiary a Schedule A from Form 8971 that states the value to use. File the appraisal with your records.

The IRS notes that basis can also change with improvements you add and with depreciation you claimed. For holding period questions on property acquired from a decedent, IRS Topic 409 points to Publication 544.

What steps should a Missouri seller take before filing?

  • Collect the closing disclosure and any Form 1099-S from the title company.
  • Add up your purchase price, closing costs at purchase and capital improvements to build the adjusted basis.
  • Test the federal exclusion with the 24 month ownership and use rules.
  • Report the sale on the federal return if the gain exceeds the exclusion or if you received a 1099-S.
  • Carry the federal capital gain amount to Form MO-A and claim the subtraction on MO-1040.
  • Check withholding. The Department of Revenue's release suggests preparers review client withholding and consider lowering it where the new subtraction applies.

Keep these records for as long as you may need to defend the return.

More questions about Missouri Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Is there a Missouri capital gains tax on real estate?

Effectively none for individuals who qualify for the subtraction. Missouri lets eligible individuals subtract 100 percent of federally reported capital gains, including real estate gains, from federal adjusted gross income. You still report the sale on your federal return.

Which Missouri form do I use to claim the capital gains subtraction?

Form MO-A, filed with Form MO-1040. The capital gain amount comes from your federal return, which for 2025 is line 7a of Form 1040.

Can a trust or LLC claim the Missouri subtraction?

Generally no. According to the department, a trust is not an individual subject to tax under section 143.011, and a pass-through entity subject to pass-through entity tax cannot claim it either.

How much of my home sale gain can I exclude on my federal return?

A single filer can leave out $250,000 and a joint return $500,000, provided you owned the home and lived in it for 24 months within the last 5 years. IRS Topic 701 and Publication 523 cover the details.

Does the Missouri subtraction cover a capital loss on my house?

No. Capital losses do not qualify for the subtraction, and the IRS treats a loss on a personal residence as nondeductible.

Which office files a Missouri deed?

The county recorder where the parcel lies. Section 442.380 requires any written instrument that conveys real estate, or touches it in law or equity, to be filed in that county's recorder office after it has been acknowledged or proved and certified.

Titles differ across Missouri. Moniteau County lets the circuit clerk act as recorder, so the office is Room 102 in the county courthouse, in the town of California, and the Missouri Association of Counties lists 573-796-2071 for it. Other counties run a stand-alone recorder of deeds. Phone the county that holds your parcel before mailing a thing.

Filing is not what makes a deed binding between the people who signed it. Section 442.400 withholds validity from an unrecorded instrument as to everyone except the parties and those with actual notice. A buyer who never files therefore leaves the purchase open to anyone who had no actual notice of it.

The recorder's job under section 59.330 reaches beyond deeds. Mortgages, deeds of trust, assignments, bonds, covenants and defeasances that concern land all belong on the same record, as do marriage contracts and certificates, so a title search can turn up several kinds of paper against one parcel.

What must a Missouri deed contain before the recorder will accept it?

It needs the grantor's signature, a proper acknowledgment, a legal description, and a mailing address for at least one grantee. Those four items come from three different statutes, so sellers often miss one.

  • Signature. Section 442.130 says the person granting the land signs, or a lawful agent signs for them.
  • Marital status. The same section requires any written instrument conveying real estate to say whether each individual grantor, mortgagor or other signer is married or unmarried.
  • Acknowledgment. The signature has to be acknowledged or proved before an authorized officer. Within the state, section 442.150 names a sealed court, its judge, justice or clerk, and notaries public. A notary in another state can take it as well.
  • Legal description and grantee address. Section 59.330 requires a legal description of the land, plus a mailing address for one grantee on every deed except easements and rights of way. A recorder is told not to file a deed missing either one, yet the statute says the instrument's validity and its constructive notice survive the omission.

The acknowledgment certificate has its own wording rules. Section 442.210 sets out sample certificates for individuals, for people signing through an attorney in fact, and for corporations, and the notary adds a signature and title at the end.

How should the pages be formatted for a Missouri recorder?

A recorder may turn away a deed over margins alone. The requirements appear in subsection 1 of section 59.310, and a title company usually handles them, but a seller preparing a quitclaim or family deed on their own should check each one.

  • Single-sided pages that are loose, not bound, with nothing stapled on unless a statute demands the attachment.
  • Print of eight points or larger, in black or dark ink, on white or light-colored paper weighing 20 pounds or more.
  • A three inch blank band across the top of page one, held for the recorder's stamp, and margins of 0.75 inch on every other edge.
  • Dark-ink signatures, each with the signer's name typed, printed or stamped underneath.

The first page, below that three inch margin, must show the document title, its date, every grantor's name and marital status, every grantee's name, any statutory addresses, the legal description, and the book and page of any referenced record. A deed that misses the format can still go on record, with a $25 surcharge. Several kinds of paper skip the format rules entirely: anything signed before 2002, military separation papers, documents executed overseas, certified copies, instruments where an original party has died or become incapacitated, and court judgments. When the recorder rejects a document, it must be returned with the reason.

What will the recorder charge on a Missouri deed?

Plan on $5 for page one and $3 for every page that follows, for any deed or instrument other than a plat or survey. A three page warranty deed therefore runs $11, before any surcharge the situation triggers.

Charges a Missouri recorder may collect under RSMo 59.310
ServiceFee
Recording a deed or other instrument$5 for page one, then $3 per page
Copy of a recorded instrumentNo more than $2 for page one, $1 per page after
Certificate and seal apart from a recording$1
Release or assignment of several items$5 for each item past the first
Subdivision or condominium plat$25 a sheet
Survey of one or more tracts$5 a sheet
Document that fails the format rules$25 added

The recorder may also set a reasonable charge for other use of equipment, staff and facilities, and for duplicate records on media other than paper. Ask the office for the total on your pages before a check goes out.

Can you record a Missouri deed electronically?

Only where the county recorder has chosen to offer it. Section 59.563 lets the recorder of deeds in any county or municipality set up an electronic format for recording and filing, and it also says no recorder has to establish, accept or transmit documents electronically.

That leaves three practical routes for a seller or buyer. Your closing agent can submit it. You can carry the paper original to the counter yourself. Or you can mail it with a check for the page charges and a return address. Whichever way you choose, call the office first and ask how it wants the deed delivered and how to make out the check.

When the deed carries a signer who has died or become incapacitated, such as a deed signed years ago and never filed, the format exemption in section 59.310 applies. Ask the recorder how they want that kind of document presented.

Why does the filing step matter when you sell for cash?

Because the buyer's title rests on it. A cash purchaser in Missouri still expects a signed, acknowledged deed to be filed in the right county, and whoever handles closing will look at what is already on record against the property.

If the house reached you through a death, the route to clean title often passes through the recorder. A beneficiary deed works only if it was already on file when the owner died, and a small estate affidavit becomes evidence of ownership once a copy is filed with the recorder of each county where the real estate sits. Our guide to Missouri beneficiary deeds builds on the same filing rules.

Before listing, pull your current vesting deed and compare its names, marital status statements and legal description against what you plan to sign. If the record and your deed disagree, ask the recorder what correction document they accept.

More questions about Missouri Recording a Deed

What does a Missouri recorder charge for a deed?

Statute sets $5 for page one and $3 for each further page, with plats and surveys priced separately. A deed that fails the format rules costs $25 more. Call the office for the exact total.

Must a Missouri deed be notarized?

It must be acknowledged or proved and certified, and a notary public can do that inside Missouri, as can a sealed court or its judge, justice or clerk. Section 442.150 lists the officers.

Does an unrecorded Missouri deed still count?

It binds the two parties and anyone who actually knew of it. Section 442.400 denies it validity against everyone else until it is deposited with the recorder, so file it quickly.

Can a Missouri recorder turn my deed down?

Yes. A deed that breaks the format rules of section 59.310, or lacks a legal description or a grantee's mailing address under section 59.330, can be refused. The rejection comes back with a stated reason.

Do I state marital status on a Missouri deed?

Yes. Section 442.130 requires every written instrument conveying real estate to say whether each individual grantor, mortgagor or other signer is married or unmarried. Place it beside the name.
